name: application/problem+json
description:
A problem details object is the standard shape for an HTTP error body, defined by RFC 9457. Instead of inventing a JSON envelope per API, a response carries `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`. The `type` member is a URI naming the kind of problem, so a client can branch on it without reading prose.

RFC 9457 replaced RFC 7807, adding a registry of common problem type URIs and guidance for type URIs that cannot be dereferenced. The same model serialised as XML is [application/problem+xml](/application/problem+xml).

furtherReading.title: RFC 9457 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs

name: application/problem+xml
description:
The XML serialisation of the problem details model from RFC 9457, the standard shape for an HTTP error body. It carries the same members as the JSON form: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`. They appear as child elements of a `problem` element in the `urn:ietf:rfc:7807` namespace.

That namespace still names the older specification, because RFC 9457 kept it unchanged when it replaced RFC 7807. Most APIs use [application/problem+json](/application/problem+json). This type exists so an XML API does not have to invent an error format of its own.

furtherReading.title: RFC 9457 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs

name: application/merge-patch+json
description:
JSON Merge Patch, defined by RFC 7396, describes a change to a JSON document by sending something that looks like the document. Members in the patch replace the ones they match, a member set to `null` is removed, and anything left out is untouched.

That shape is easy to write and easy to get wrong. It cannot address a single array element and cannot express a precondition. It also has no way to set a member to `null`, because `null` already means delete. When any of that matters, [application/json-patch+json](/application/json-patch+json) spells each operation out instead.

name: application/json-seq
description:
A JSON text sequence is any number of JSON values in one stream, as defined by RFC 7464. Each value is preceded by an ASCII record separator (0x1E) and followed by a line feed. The separator cannot appear unescaped inside a JSON text, so a reader can always find where the next value starts.

That suits a long or never-ending sequence that would be awkward as a single enormous array. A consumer handles each value as it arrives instead of waiting for a closing bracket, and one malformed value need not be fatal. `jq` reads and writes it with the `--seq` flag.

furtherReading.title: RFC 7464 - JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Text Sequences

name: application/jsonpath
description:
JSONPath selects values out of a JSON document. An expression starts at the root `$` and applies segments. So `$.store.book[*].author` picks the author of every book, and `$..price` finds every price at any depth.

The syntax began as Stefan Gössner's 2007 proposal. Dozens of libraries implemented it long before anyone wrote it down, which left them quietly incompatible with each other. RFC 9535 is the specification that fixes that, and this media type is registered for carrying a query, not the values it returns.

furtherReading.title: RFC 9535 - JSONPath: Query Expressions for JSON

name: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
description:
This is what an HTML form posts by default. Each name and value is percent-encoded, pairs are joined with `&`, name is separated from value by `=`, and a space is written as `+`. It is older than most of this list, and is specified today in the WHATWG URL Standard rather than in HTML itself.

The `+` is the part people get wrong, since percent-encoding elsewhere writes a space as `%20`. The format also has no way to carry a file, which is what multipart/form-data exists for. Its registration gives no file extension, because it is only ever sent in a message and never saved as a file.
